newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan police find bottle of cult's deadly VX gas.
newsitem.headline: Japan police find bottle of cult's deadly VX gas.

text.p: Japanese police unearthed a bottle of the deadly nerve gas VX after a confession and directions supplied by an incarcerated member of the Aum Shinri Kyo doomsday cult, a police spokesman said.
Investigators were taken to a spot on a river bank in Kodaira, a western suburb of Tokyo, by Yasuo Hayashi, a senior member of Aum Shinri Kyo (Supreme Truth Sect), the spokesman said.
They found a tightly sealed glass bottle containing about 40 millilitres (about 1.4 British fluid ounces) of VX in liquid form. The bottle was placed inside a metal can.

Hayashi, dubbed the "killing machine" by the Japanese media for his suspected involvement in a host of alleged crimes committee by the cult, was arrested last week on the southern island of Ishigakijima with a female cult member after a year on the run.
Hayashi was arrested on murder charges stemming from the March 1995 Tokyo subway nerve gas attack, which killed 12 people and made 6,000 ill.
VX, developed by U.S. and British chemists in the 1950s, is several times more powerful than sarin, the gas used in the Tokyo subway attack.
One drop of VX on the skin can kill a person immediately by paralysing the body's entire nervous system, thus preventing the person from breathing.

Police refused to comment on how Hayashi knew the location of the bottle or whether anyone else knew of it. But the spokesman said police have now recovered all VX made by cult scientist Masami Tsuchiya over the years.
Prosecutors have charged cult guru Shoko Asahara with directing the Tokyo subway attack and involvement in three separate murder and attempted murder cases using VX gas.
Asahara has been accused of 17 separate crimes, but has not entered a plea for any of them.
In one case, a cult member, suspected of spying for police, died just minutes after a drop of VX was placed on the back of his neck from a syringe as he was walking down a street in May 1994.
All but two cult members accused of carrying out the subway attack and other murder cases have been arrested.
In an annual report released on Thursday, Japan's national police force said the cult was continuing to operate despite being declared bankrupt.
In its 1996 report on public security, the National Police Agency said the cult changed the names of companies it runs and made its followers live together in small groups in apartments.
Each group, with its own leader, contacts other groups using personal computer networks, the report said. Cult guru Asahara remains the cult's supreme leader, it said.

The cult may soon be disbanded under a controversial anti-subversion law. The Public Security Commission, a panel of seven jurists, scholars and media personnel, is to make a final decision on the disbandment order early next year.
